How is Mississippi organized when you sell a house here?

Mississippi has 82 counties and 299 municipalities, and almost every step of a home sale runs through a county office. The records, the tax bill and any court file all sit with the county where the house stands, so that is the first place to look.

Each county is governed by a five-member Board of Supervisors. The chancery clerk keeps land records, the tax assessor values property, and the tax collector sends the bill. In 23 counties the assessor and collector are separate officials. Two of the counties we cover, Hinds and Harrison, have two county seats, so the right courthouse can depend on which part of the county the house is in.

Size varies a lot. Harrison County is the most populous at 217,136 people in 2025 estimates, while Issaquena County has 1,263. Six counties have more than 100,000 residents, including Hinds, DeSoto, Rankin and Jackson. Sellers in the big metro counties usually deal with busy offices, and sellers in rural counties may need to call ahead.

What does property tax look like for a Mississippi seller?

Tax is the true value of the property times an assessment ratio times the millage rate. The Department of Revenue splits property into five classes, and a house you live in sits in the lowest one.

ClassPropertyAssessment ratio
ISingle-family, owner-occupied residential real property10%
IIAll other real property15%
IIIPersonal property, with exceptions15%
IVPublic utility property30%
VMotor vehicles30%

The state's own example uses a $100,000 value, a 10% ratio and 125 mills, which comes to $1,250. A mill is one thousandth of a dollar. Every property pays a county rate and a school district rate, and a house inside city limits pays the city rate as well.

Taxes are assessed to the owner of record on January 1, billed in November and December, and due by February 1. Real property must be revalued at least once every four years. If you disagree with a value, you can ask the Board of Supervisors for a hearing, and the appeal normally has to be filed by the first Monday in August before the tax comes due. The chancery clerk can explain how your county handles it. Our Mississippi property tax guide goes deeper.

Unpaid tax is the part that surprises sellers. Penalties and interest build, and a delinquent property can go to the county tax auction, held on the first Monday in April in some counties and the last Monday in August in others. Ask the tax collector for the current balance before you set a closing date.

Does the homestead exemption affect a sale?

Yes, because it belongs to the owner and not to the house. Applications go to the county tax assessor between January 1 and April 1, and the applicant must own and live in the home on January 1.

  • Tier 1 is a tax credit of up to $300 for applicants under 65.
  • Tier 2 covers people 65 or older, or totally disabled, and exempts the first $7,500 of assessed value.
  • Tier 3 is a total exemption for certain disabled veterans, veterans 90 or older, and some unremarried surviving spouses.

A deed change, a divorce or a death can require a new application, and the ownership paper must be on file with the chancery clerk before January 7. A buyer who plans to live in the house has to apply on their own. A seller who moved out and now rents the house should not assume the exemption continues. Details are in our homestead exemption guide.

How does foreclosure work in Mississippi?

Most Mississippi home loans use a deed of trust, and the statute on those sales sets a short public timeline. Under Section 89-1-55 of the Mississippi Code, land sold under a deed of trust is sold at public outcry in the county where it sits, or in the county where the borrower lives.

The sale must be advertised for three consecutive weeks in a newspaper published in the county, and a notice must also be posted at the courthouse. Both must name the original borrower. A sale that skips the advertising is not valid, whatever the contract says.

So an owner who gets a notice of sale has weeks, not months, to act. A seller can still close a normal sale before the auction date, and a cash buyer can purchase as-is when repairs or a messy payment history would scare off a bank-financed buyer. Ask the lender for a payoff figure and the sale date in writing, and speak with a Mississippi real estate attorney about your own file. Our statute source does not cover redemption or deficiency rules, so we leave those to your attorney.

What happens when you inherit a Mississippi house?

Probate runs through chancery court, and the chancery clerk's office keeps both the estate file and the land records. Heirs usually start there, since the clerk can say where an estate is filed and what a deed will cost to record.

Mississippi has no inheritance tax and no gift tax, and the Department of Revenue says no state estate tax return is required for deaths on or after January 1, 2005. Federal rules still apply to very large estates, and income tax on any gain after the sale is a question for a tax professional.

Creditors have a defined window. Under Section 91-7-145, the executor or administrator mails notice to known creditors, then publishes a notice in a county newspaper for three consecutive weeks. A claim not probated and registered within 90 days after the first publication is barred. Heirs planning a sale should expect that clock to run before they see net proceeds.

  • Find out which chancery court holds the estate.
  • Confirm who has authority to sign a deed.
  • Ask the tax collector whether any year is unpaid.
  • Get a date-of-death value in writing for the sale file.

Our guides on Mississippi probate and estate and inheritance tax cover the steps in more detail.

What should you know about deeds and recording fees?

Deeds are recorded with the chancery clerk of the county where the land lies. The Harrison County clerk's schedule, based on Section 25-7-9 and effective January 1, 2020, lists a deed at $26 in counties that collect the $1 archive fee and $25 in those that do not, for the first five pages, plus $1 for each extra page.

CountyCollects archive feeDeed, first five pages
HindsYes$26
HarrisonYes$26
RankinYes$26
LowndesYes$26
DeSotoNot listed$25
LafayetteNot listed$25
ForrestNot listed$25

Treat these as a starting point, since the clerk works out the final amount at filing. The clerk's schedule says nothing about a state transfer tax, so ask your closing agent or the clerk what applies to your sale. Our quitclaim deed guide explains recording order and format rules.

What if the house has tenants?

Rented houses fall under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, Title 89, Chapter 8. Unless a lease sets a fixed term, the tenancy is week to week for a tenant who pays weekly and month to month for everyone else.

Either side can end a month-to-month tenancy with written notice at least 30 days before the end date, and a week-to-week tenancy with at least seven days. A landlord who wants a vacant house for closing should count those days into the schedule. A court judgment is still the route when a tenant will not leave, so do not change locks or cut utilities. Our Mississippi eviction guide walks through the court steps.

A rented house is usually taxed in Class II at 15%, not the 10% owner-occupied rate, so check the bill if you moved out and rented.

What does a cash sale as-is mean in Mississippi?

It means the buyer takes the house in its current condition and you skip the repair list, showings and lender appraisal. Closing still runs through a title company or attorney, who confirms the owner, searches the chancery clerk's records and pays off liens and back taxes from the proceeds.

That makes the paperwork the real timeline. A clean title and a current tax bill close quickly, while an open estate, an unrecorded deed or a delinquent tax year take time to fix. We buy houses in Mississippi as-is and reply with a written offer, and we make no promise on price before we know the title and condition. Frequently asked questions

How many counties does Mississippi have?

Mississippi has 82 counties and 299 municipalities. Property records, tax bills and probate files are handled at the county level, so start with the county where the house sits.

When are Mississippi property taxes due?

Taxes are assessed to the owner of record on January 1, billed in November and December, and due by February 1 of the following year. Unpaid tax can lead to the county tax auction.

Who do I call about a property tax bill?

Call the county tax collector for the bill and the balance owed. The tax assessor handles value, and the chancery clerk can explain how to appeal to the Board of Supervisors.

How long is the foreclosure notice in Mississippi?

A sale under a deed of trust must be advertised for three consecutive weeks in a county newspaper and posted at the courthouse. Ask your lender and an attorney about your own sale date.

Does Mississippi have an inheritance tax?

No. The Department of Revenue says the state has no inheritance or gift tax, and no state estate tax return is required for deaths on or after January 1, 2005.

Can I sell an inherited house before probate ends?

You need someone with legal authority to sign. Check with the chancery clerk where the estate is filed, and note that creditors have 90 days from first publication to file claims.

How much notice does a landlord give a month-to-month tenant?

At least 30 days in writing under Section 89-8-19. A week-to-week tenancy needs at least seven days.

Will you buy a house with back taxes or tenants?

We buy as-is, including houses with tax due, deferred repairs or tenants. Send us the address and we will review the title and condition before we reply in writing.
